explanation: Stegosaurus had died out by about 145 million years ago. T. rex lived around 68 to 66 million years ago, so less time separates it from us than from Stegosaurus.

claims.text: The time between Stegosaurus and Tyrannosaurus rex is greater than the time between Tyrannosaurus rex and the present day.
Stegosaurus lived in the Late Jurassic and had died out by about 145 million years ago.
Tyrannosaurus rex lived about 68 to 66 million years ago.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Gap: The AMNH states that the amount of time between Stegosaurus and T. rex is 80 million years. ... Tyrannosaurus rex: Estimates vary by source. The Smithsonian gives 67–66 million years ago, the American Museum of Natural History gives 69 to 66 million years ago, and Britannica gives about 80 million and 66 million years ago for the known fossils.

claimResults.note: The AMNH's statement of an 80-million-year gap supports the key. But this call and the two follow-ups counted here (W9; W10, a Britannica-only call, query 'Tyrannosaurus rex lived how many million years ago, Late Cretaceous, Britannica') report Britannica dating T. rex to about 80 to 66 million years ago (its tyrannosaur article) and about 100 to 66 million (its main entry). On those figures an early T. rex would sit closer to Stegosaurus, which Britannica ends at about 144 million, than to us, so Tier B sources disagree on the key's premise (§9.5.2). My own view: the dated specimens (Trix about 67 million, Peter about 66.8, Tufts-Love about 66.3) and the late Maastrichtian formations make 68 to 66 million right, and the statement true.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: T. rex lived near the end of the Cretaceous, in the late Maastrichtian, roughly 66 to 68 million years ago. Stage and dates: Wikipedia places the fossil-bearing formations in the late Maastrichtian, 69 to 66 million years ago. Its later discussion gives the established Maastrichtian range as about 68–66 Ma. Broader estimates: Britannica gives a wider window, about 80 million and 66 million years ago. That lower bound reaches back into the Campanian, and the broader range is likely why some sources differ.

claimResults.note: Wikipedia, AMNH and the Smithsonian give about 69 or 68 to 66 million years; Britannica gives 80 to 66 (and W10 adds a 100 to 66 span on its main T. rex entry). Sources disagree, so the claim fails as written.

issues.note: Sources disagree on when T. rex lived: Wikipedia, AMNH and the Smithsonian give about 69 or 68 to 66 million years ago, Britannica 80 to 66 (about 100 to 66 on its main entry). The statement and the explanation's '68 to 66 million years ago' therefore fail as written under §9.5.2. A wording every source supports: 'The last T. rex lived closer in time to us than to the last Stegosaurus' (about 66 against about 145 million years ago). Or a tiebreak could weigh the dated specimens and the AMNH's 80-million-year gap.

issues.note: Read with Stegosaurus in its usual sense, the Late Jurassic genus, the statement holds by a wide margin (at least 77 against at most 68 million years). Some taxonomists have proposed folding the Early Cretaceous stegosaur Wuerhosaurus into Stegosaurus as S. homheni, which could undo the comparison under that very broad reading of the genus. The statement and explanation plainly mean the Late Jurassic animal, so no change is needed.
